questions.question: In the CUDA programming model, what best describes the relationship between threads, warps, blocks, and grids?
questions.choice_A: Threads are grouped into grids, grids are grouped into warps, and warps into blocks.
questions.choice_B: Threads are grouped into warps, warps into blocks, and blocks into a grid for a kernel launch.
questions.choice_C: Blocks are grouped into threads, threads into grids, and grids into warps.
questions.choice_D: Warps are independent of threads but are coordinated by grids, which are assigned to blocks.

questions.question: Which memory type on NVIDIA GPUs offers the lowest latency but the smallest capacity and is private to each thread?
questions.choice_A: Registers
questions.choice_B: Global memory
questions.choice_C: Shared memory
questions.choice_D: Constant memory

questions.question: What is the primary goal of coalesced global memory access?
questions.choice_A: To ensure all threads in a block share the same memory address.
questions.choice_B: To avoid register spilling by increasing register allocation.
questions.choice_C: To combine per-thread memory transactions into fewer, wider transactions that match the memory bus width.
questions.choice_D: To guarantee that every warp executes the same instruction path without divergence.

questions.question: On NVIDIA GPUs, why is warp-level execution relevant when designing a kernel?
questions.choice_A: Warps control the occupancy directly by setting the number of SMs.
questions.choice_B: Threads within a warp execute in lockstep, so divergence causes serialization and performance loss.
questions.choice_C: Warps determine the size of shared memory per block.
questions.choice_D: Warp size dynamically changes based on the kernel’s register usage.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes shared memory compared to global memory?
questions.choice_A: Shared memory is slower but larger than global memory and is read-only.
questions.choice_B: Shared memory is faster, on-chip, programmer-managed, and scoped to a block.
questions.choice_C: Shared memory is accessible only by a single thread and is automatically cached.
questions.choice_D: Shared memory has the same latency as registers but is globally visible.

questions.question: What is a common cause of shared memory bank conflicts?
questions.choice_A: Using too many registers per thread.
questions.choice_B: Accessing memory with a stride that maps multiple threads in a warp to the same bank.
questions.choice_C: Launching too many thread blocks per SM.
questions.choice_D: Using constant memory for frequently changing values.

questions.question: When implementing a custom matrix multiplication kernel, why is tiling into shared memory beneficial?
questions.choice_A: It reduces the number of registers required per thread.
questions.choice_B: It maximizes occupancy by reducing block size.
questions.choice_C: It increases data reuse and reduces costly global memory traffic.
questions.choice_D: It eliminates the need for synchronization within a block.

questions.question: What is the primary performance trade-off when increasing per-thread register usage?
questions.choice_A: Higher register usage always increases memory bandwidth.
questions.choice_B: Higher register usage can reduce occupancy, potentially lowering the ability to hide latency.
questions.choice_C: Higher register usage eliminates the need for shared memory.
questions.choice_D: Higher register usage guarantees elimination of bank conflicts.

questions.question: For low-bit (e.g., 4-bit) compute kernels, which approach is typically necessary to achieve high throughput on general-purpose CUDA cores?
questions.choice_A: Storing each 4-bit value in a separate 32-bit float to simplify arithmetic.
questions.choice_B: Packing multiple low-bit elements into wider words and using bitwise ops to unpack/accumulate.
questions.choice_C: Converting all low-bit values to double precision before multiply-accumulate.
questions.choice_D: Avoiding shared memory because it cannot store packed data.

questions.question: Which statement about constant memory is accurate?
questions.choice_A: It is large and best for streaming large arrays of data per thread.
questions.choice_B: It has similar latency to global memory and no caching behavior.
questions.choice_C: It is cached and very efficient when all threads in a warp read the same address (broadcast).
questions.choice_D: It is writable by device code to update parameters mid-kernel.

questions.question: How does occupancy generally impact performance?
questions.choice_A: Higher occupancy always yields higher performance regardless of access patterns.
questions.choice_B: Higher occupancy increases the number of active warps, which can help hide latency but may not overcome poor memory access patterns.
questions.choice_C: Lower occupancy always eliminates memory divergence.
questions.choice_D: Occupancy only affects shared memory performance and not compute throughput.

questions.question: What is a practical method to avoid shared memory bank conflicts for a 2D tile stored row-major?
questions.choice_A: Use a tile width that is a multiple of the number of banks with no padding.
questions.choice_B: Interleave rows and columns in a checkerboard pattern.
questions.choice_C: Pad each row by one element so consecutive rows start at different banks.
questions.choice_D: Use only even thread indices to access shared memory.

questions.question: When profiling a CUDA kernel with Nsight Compute, which metric pattern most strongly suggests uncoalesced global loads?
questions.choice_A: High SM occupancy and high FLOP utilization.
questions.choice_B: Low memory transaction count and high L2 hit rate.
questions.choice_C: High number of memory transactions per requested byte and low global load efficiency.
questions.choice_D: High Tensor Core utilization with balanced L2 traffic.

questions.question: In custom matmul kernels tuned for modern NVIDIA GPUs, which strategy aligns best with hardware characteristics?
questions.choice_A: Launch one thread per output matrix and compute all elements serially.
questions.choice_B: Use block-level tiling with per-thread subtiles and register blocking to increase reuse.
questions.choice_C: Avoid using shared memory to reduce synchronization costs.
questions.choice_D: Use only scalar loads and stores to prevent bank conflicts.

questions.question: What is an advantage of using Tensor Cores (via WMMA or CUTLASS) for low-bit or mixed-precision matmul when available?
questions.choice_A: They automatically coalesce all global memory accesses without programmer effort.
questions.choice_B: They eliminate the need for synchronization within a warp.
questions.choice_C: They can provide significantly higher throughput for supported data types and tile sizes.
questions.choice_D: They remove the need for any shared memory usage in all cases.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes nvprof from modern Nsight tools?
questions.choice_A: nvprof is the newest tool for detailed kernel-level analysis and roofline modeling.
questions.choice_B: Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute have superseded nvprof, offering system-level tracing and kernel-level metrics, respectively.
questions.choice_C: nvprof is required for profiling Tensor Cores and low-bit operations.
questions.choice_D: Nsight tools cannot collect GPU performance counters.

questions.question: When integrating a custom CUDA kernel as a PyTorch extension, which practice is most important for correctness and performance?
questions.choice_A: Always copy tensors to host before kernel launch to ensure alignment.
questions.choice_B: Rely on Python’s GIL to synchronize CUDA streams.
questions.choice_C: Validate tensor dtype, device, contiguity, and layout, and launch on the current CUDA stream.
questions.choice_D: Use only default streams to avoid any race conditions.

questions.question: Which scenario most likely causes register spilling to local memory and hurts performance?
questions.choice_A: Using fewer threads per block than the maximum.
questions.choice_B: Exceeding available registers per thread due to large temporaries or aggressive unrolling.
questions.choice_C: Padding shared memory tiles to avoid bank conflicts.
questions.choice_D: Using constant memory for small read-only parameters.

questions.question: In a low-bit GEMM kernel that packs 8 signed 4-bit values into a 32-bit integer, what is a typical step before accumulation?
questions.choice_A: Convert the packed integer to a double and multiply directly with floats.
questions.choice_B: Perform bitwise shifts and masks to extract sub-4-bit lanes, then sign-extend to a wider integer type.
questions.choice_C: Use atomic adds on each 4-bit lane stored in global memory.
questions.choice_D: Transpose the entire matrix in global memory to ensure alignment.

questions.question: What is a common pitfall when designing thread/block dimensions for a tiled matmul kernel?
questions.choice_A: Choosing block sizes that map cleanly to warp multiples.
questions.choice_B: Using per-thread subtiles to increase data reuse.
questions.choice_C: Setting tile sizes that exceed shared memory or register limits per block, reducing occupancy or causing spills.
questions.choice_D: Aligning global memory accesses to 128-bit boundaries.

questions.question: When using GPU performance counters to diagnose a kernel bottleneck, which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.choice_A: High achieved occupancy guarantees the kernel is compute-bound.
questions.choice_B: High memory throughput approaching device peak with low compute utilization suggests memory-bound behavior.
questions.choice_C: Low L2 traffic always indicates perfect cache utilization.
questions.choice_D: High SM busy percentage always implies optimal instruction scheduling.
